title: Why was he so smart?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Albert Einstein is considered a genius by most people, and the scientific discoveries he made transformed the way we see the universe. Now a study of 14 newly discovered photographs of his brain has concluded that it was indeed unusual in many ways, but researchers stop short of drawing a direct link between the organ's extra folds and convolutions and Einstein's brilliance. 'Shark-fin shaped knobs and ridges seldom seen in other people's brains were there,' they observe. However, since we still don't know enough about the brain to understand how these folds might translate into Einstein's unique abilities, the researchers are unable to provide an answer to this question at this time.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The story begins in 1955, the year Einstein died. A pathologist named Thomas Harvey was given the job of performing the autopsy. Harvey later said he felt compelled to preserve the great man's brain. He photographed it from numerous angles and then cut it into 240 blocks, which he embedded in a resin-like substance known as celloidin. He then cut the blocks into as many as 2,000 thin sections and mounted them on microscope slides. Over the decades, he distributed some of the slides to at least 18 researchers.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Harvey also noticed that Einstein had no parietal operculum in either hemisphere. But no peer-reviewed studies were published until 1985, and only six have appeared since. Early studies found that in a region of the parietal lobe that is related to mathematical reasoning, Einstein had a greater density of neurons. A study in 1996 found that Einstein had a higher ratio of glia (cells that help neurons pass and receive information) to neurons in some brain regions. In 2009, Dean Falk, an evolutionary anthropologist at Florida State University in Tallahassee, published a study based on Harvey's photographs, in which she found, among other things, unusual patterns of ridges and grooves in the parietal lobes.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: However, the earlier study was based on only a handful of photographs. In 2010, Harvey's heirs transferred all of his holdings to the US Army's National Museum of Health and Medicine in Silver Spring, Maryland. Working with the museum, Falk and her team analysed 14 photographs that had never been published before in a study which appeared in the journal Brain.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The team compared Einstein's brain with those of 85 other people whose brains have been described in prior studies. They found that Einstein's brain weighed 1,230 grams, which is within the normal range. But the brain had some unusual features. There were additional convolutions and folds (in the right prefrontal cortex, the parietal lobes and the visual cortex) compared with the 85 other brains. Furthermore, some regions on the left side of the brain which relate to sensing and controlling the face, tongue, and larynx were greatly enlarged. In addition, Einstein's prefrontal cortex, which is related to planning, attention and perseverance in the face of challenges, was greatly expanded.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Albert Galaburda, a neuroscientist at Harvard Medical School who was not involved in the study, found the research 'richly' interesting, but said it raises many unanswered questions. 'Is it Einstein's birth-given brain or the fact that he played a lot of physics that gave him a different brain?' The answer is we don't know, he says. 'We still don't know what makes a genius,' Galaburda adds, but he suspects it's a combination of the brain a person is born with and what happens during the course of their life. 'It's the shark fin that catches the right wave.'

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Falk agrees that both nature and nurture were involved. She points out that Einstein's parents enrolled him in violin lessons at the age of five, and also bought him a piano. That led to a lifelong passion for music and passion for something seems to be the key. A region in Einstein's brain that is generally related to creative pursuits such as music was 'incredibly expansive,' Falk says. 'Einstein programmed his own brain,' she suggests.
